statement: The supplied sources do not contain a derivation of the final value theorem (only conditions, statements, counterexamples, and a proof of an Abelian theorem are given; the derivative-based theorem has no derivation supplied). As stated in the sources, the standard Final Value Theorem relates a frequency-domain Laplace transform F(s) to the asymptotic time-domain behavior of f(t): if every pole of F(s) is in the open left half-plane or at the origin, and F(s) has at most a single pole at the origin, then \lim_{t \to \infty} f(t) = \lim_{s \to 0} s F(s). Under the formulation using the Laplace transform of the derivative, if f(t) and f'(t) have Laplace transforms existing for all s > 0, and both \lim_{t \to \infty} f(t) and \lim_{s \to 0} s F(s) exist, then \lim_{t \to \infty} f(t) = \lim_{s \to 0} s F(s).

symbols.meaning: limiting value in C or R
limiting value or asymptotic mean in C
growth exponent in the generalized theorem with \lambda > -1

properties.property: If f : (0, \infty) \to \mathbb{C} is bounded and measurable with \lim_{t \to \infty} f(t) = \alpha \in \mathbb{C}, then F(s) exists for all s > 0 and \lim_{s \downarrow 0} s F(s) = \alpha.
properties.why: the Abelian Final Value Theorem guarantees that convergence in the time domain induces convergence of the Laplace transform scaled by s as s approaches 0 from above

properties.property: If f : (0, \infty) \to \mathbb{C} is bounded and differentiable, t f'(t) is bounded on (0, \infty), and s F(s) \to L \in \mathbb{C} as s \to 0, then \lim_{t \to \infty} f(t) = L.
properties.why: the Tauberian converse condition on t f'(t) prevents high-frequency oscillations that would otherwise allow s F(s) to converge while f(t) fails to settle

properties.property: If F(s) is a proper rational function with all poles in the open left half-plane or at the origin, then s F(s) \to L \in \mathbb{R} as s \downarrow 0 implies f(t) \to L, while s F(s) \to \pm\infty implies f(t) \to \pm\infty.
properties.why: extended rational function analysis accounts for multiple poles at the origin leading to polynomial unbounded divergence

properties.property: If f(t) is Laplace transformable, \lambda > -1, and both limits exist, then \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{f(t)}{t^\lambda} = \frac{1}{\Gamma(\lambda + 1)} \lim_{s \downarrow 0} s^{\lambda + 1} F(s).
properties.why: generalized final value theorems relate polynomial asymptotic growth rates t^\lambda to frequency-domain scaling by s^{\lambda + 1}

properties.property: If f is continuously differentiable, f' is absolutely integrable on (0, \infty), and \lim_{t \to \infty} f(t) exists and is finite, then \lim_{s \to 0^+} s F(s) = \lim_{t \to \infty} f(t).
properties.why: dominated convergence allows passing the limit as s \to 0^+ under the integral sign of the derivative's transform

properties.property: If f is continuous and bounded on (0, \infty) and its Cesàro mean limit \lim_{T \to \infty} \frac{1}{T} \int_0^T f(t) dt = \alpha exists, then \lim_{s \to 0, s > 0} s F(s) = \alpha.
properties.why: the final value limit of s F(s) extracts the average value over time even when f(t) itself does not converge pointwise

assumptions.assumption: All poles of F(s) must lie in the open left half-plane, with at most a single simple pole at the origin s = 0.
assumptions.breaks_when: F(s) has poles in the open right half-plane, imaginary-axis poles other than the origin, or multiple poles at s = 0.

assumptions.assumption: The time-domain limit \lim_{t \to \infty} f(t) must exist for the standard and derivative-based bidirectional statements.
assumptions.breaks_when: f(t) oscillates persistently as t \to \infty (such as sinusoidal signals) without converging.

assumptions.assumption: Laplace transforms of both f(t) and f'(t) must exist for all s > 0.
assumptions.breaks_when: f(t) or f'(t) exhibits faster-than-exponential growth as t \to \infty.

assumptions.assumption: The derivative f'(t) must be absolutely integrable on (0, \infty) in the dominated convergence formulation.

failure_modes.mode: Undamped persistent oscillations in time domain
failure_modes.signature: \lim_{s \to 0} s F(s) exists and equals a finite constant, but \lim_{t \to \infty} f(t) does not exist.
failure_modes.cause: Poles on the imaginary axis (e.g., f(t) = \sin(t) with poles at s = \pm i), where \lim_{s \to 0} s F(s) = \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{s^2}{s^2+1} = 0 despite f(t) oscillating indefinitely.

failure_modes.signature: s F(s) \to \pm\infty as s \downarrow 0 and f(t) diverges to \pm\infty as t \to \infty.
failure_modes.cause: A pole of order two or higher at s = 0 generates polynomial growth in t (e.g., ramp signals), preventing convergence to a finite value.

failure_modes.mode: False converse inference without Tauberian conditions
failure_modes.signature: \lim_{s \to 0} s F(s) converges to L, but f(t) fails to converge to L as t \to \infty.
failure_modes.cause: Rapid oscillations where the derivative condition that t f'(t) is bounded on (0, \infty) is violated.
